readerTitle: Why a big goal is not a strategy
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Richard Rumelt의 좋은 전략·나쁜 전략 구분) + 가상 사례 (청소 서비스 회사 두 곳, 소프트웨어 회사의 고객지원팀)
insight: 좋은 전략은 목표를 말하는 것이 아니라 가장 중요한 문제를 진단하고, 그 문제를 푸는 방향과 서로 맞물린 행동을 정하는 것이다.
misconception: 야심찬 목표와 멋진 가치 문장을 정하면 전략을 세운 것이다. 할 일 목록이 길수록 전략이 탄탄하다.

sources.text: Rumelt, R. (2011). Good Strategy/Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters. Crown Business.
Rumelt, R. (2011). The perils of bad strategy. McKinsey Quarterly.
청소 회사와 고객지원팀 사례, 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Rumelt의 좋은 전략 핵심 3요소(diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions)와 나쁜 전략의 4가지 특징(fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, bad strategic objectives)의 표현을 원서로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 쉬운 말로 풀어 썼습니다.
청소 회사 두 곳(Bright, Tidy)과 고객지원팀의 '문의 40%가 결제 페이지 관련' 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 사례입니다. 실제 업계 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 illustrative 라벨을 유지하세요.

cards.title: Why a big goal is not a strategy
body: Two house-cleaning companies in the same town have the same problem: customers quit after a few months.
Both owners sit down to write a plan for the year. One writes a goal. The other writes down the problem. A year later, only one of them has fixed it.

image.label: Two owners writing plans at two desks
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면을 반으로 나눠 두 청소 회사 사장이 각자 책상에서 계획을 쓰는 장면. 왼쪽 메모에는 큰 글씨로 "Grow 30%!", 오른쪽 메모에는 "Why do customers leave?". 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which plan would you back?
body: You run a cleaning company. Many customers cancel after three or four visits. Three plans are on the table.

options.text: Become the town's #1 cleaning brand. Grow revenue 30%. Live our values: quality, trust, care.
options.feedback: It inspires and everyone agrees with it. But it never says why customers leave, so nobody knows what to do differently on Monday.

options.text: Cut prices 15%, hire a salesperson, launch a new website and add window cleaning.
options.feedback: Real actions, and some may help. But they don't aim at one problem, so money and attention spread thin while the cancellations continue.

options.text: Customers leave when a new cleaner shows up each time. So: same cleaner every visit. Smaller service zones to keep routes stable, and a bonus for cleaners who stay a year.
options.feedback: It names a cause, picks one direction and lines up actions behind it. It might be wrong, but you'll quickly learn whether it is.

cards.title: One plan named the problem. One didn't.
body: Bright Cleaning chose plan A. Staff liked the new slogan. Cancellations stayed the same, and the 30% target slipped quietly out of meetings by summer.
Tidy Homes chose plan C. Shrinking zones meant saying no to some far-away jobs. But regular customers now opened the door to a familiar face who knew where the spare key was. Fewer of them left.
Same town, same problem. The difference was not effort. It was **whether the plan faced the problem**.

cards.title: Good strategy vs bad strategy
body: Strategy writer Richard Rumelt argues that **good strategy** has three parts that work together:
Bad strategy often skips the first part. It sounds bold but never says what is actually in the way.
list: **Diagnosis:** what is the hardest problem we face, and why?
**Guiding policy:** our overall approach to that problem
**Coherent actions:** steps that support each other and carry out the approach

image.label: Three linked blocks: diagnosis, approach, actions
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 블록 세 개가 화살표로 이어짐: "Diagnosis: new cleaner every time" → "Approach: same cleaner every visit" → "Actions: smaller zones, retention bonus". 깔끔한 플랫 스타일, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four signs of bad strategy
body: Rumelt describes four common signs. Plan A at Bright had most of them.
list: **Fluff:** big words that sound smart but say little
**Ducking the challenge:** never naming the real problem
**Goals posing as strategy:** "grow 30%" is a wish, not a way
**A wish list:** many unrelated aims with no clear priority
cards.callout: Quick test: if any rival could sign your plan unchanged, it isn't a strategy yet.

cards.title: Bad strategy is easier to agree on.
body: Naming the real problem is uncomfortable. It may point at a team, a habit or the owner's favorite idea. A goal offends no one.
Choosing one approach also means saying no to others, like Tidy turning down far-away jobs. A long list lets everyone keep their project.
So bad strategy is rarely laziness. It is usually **avoiding a hard choice**.

cards.title: A good diagnosis can still be wrong.
body: Tidy guessed that changing cleaners drove people away. If the real cause had been price, the plan would have missed.
Treat your diagnosis as a bet. Check it early: ask customers who left, and watch whether the actions move the number.
And goals still matter. A target like "30% growth" is useful for measuring progress. It just can't tell you how to get there.

cards.title: Now it's a support team inside a software company.
body: You lead customer support at a software company. Users wait two days for answers, and churn is rising. You look closer: about 40% of tickets ask the same thing about a confusing billing page.
Your boss asks for next year's strategy. Which do you bring?

options.text: Deliver world-class support. Answer 95% of tickets within two hours.
options.feedback: A clear target, but no path to it. The same billing questions will keep flooding in.

options.text: Hire four agents, add a chatbot, open weekend shifts and rebuild the help center.
options.feedback: This may cut wait times, at a real cost. But it handles more tickets instead of asking why they arrive.

options.text: Fix causes, not volume. Work with the product team to redesign the billing page, publish one clear guide, and track repeat questions weekly.
options.feedback: It starts from the diagnosis and every action points at it. It needs another team's help, which is harder to win than a hiring budget.

cards.title: Name the problem before you name the goal.
body: Good strategy says what's in the way, how you'll get around it and which actions follow. A goal alone is only a wish.
**Try it today:** write your plan for this year in three lines: the hardest problem, your approach to it, and three actions that support each other.
